title: Your name
description: Say who you are, and how you are doing.
grammarNote: Me llamo means my name is. It is how you introduce yourself. The verbs behind these phrases, ser and estar, arrive in A1.

explanation.summary: Two questions cover almost every first meeting: what is your name, and how are you. Spanish has a fixed way of asking both.

sections.heading: Asking and answering the name
sections.body: The question is cómo te llamas, literally how do you call yourself. The answer is me llamo, and it is followed by the name: me llamo Ana. There is also the shorter yo soy, but me llamo is the ordinary way to introduce yourself.

sections.heading: How are you
sections.body: Cómo estás asks how you are. The answer is short: estoy bien, I am well. Estoy mal is I am badly. You can add a reason with porque: estoy bien, porque hace buen tiempo.

examples.en: I am not well: I am tired.

sections.heading: How much, and how many
sections.body: Mucho and poco are the two amounts you need. They are used on their own: mucho, poco. Before a noun they take the article: mucha agua, poco tiempo. The verb for have is tener, which is irregular: tengo, tienes, tiene.

examples.en: I have a lot of water.

examples.es: También hablo un poco de inglés.
examples.en: I also speak a little English.

items.note: What is your name. You answer: me llamo...
My name is. Me llamo Ana.
How are you. You answer: estoy bien.
A lot. It becomes mucha before a feminine noun.
A little. It becomes poca before a feminine noun.
See you later. You say it when you leave.
You are welcome. The answer to thank you.
